I’ve really given this game a chance, but is not what it seems. Despite being presumably gigantic, is actually pretty poor in content. All resources look the same way on each planet, all the structures found on planets look the same way (I’ve found the same 3 types of aliens all across the explored universe). Even if somehow the planets are different (with different plants and ridiculous looking animals), you can feel that basically they are the same stuff. Also I’ve found that many of the animals start to look the same way after you’ve explored a number of planets. Also the space stations look EXACTLY the same in all solar systems. So bottom line, this game had been better off if the developers hand-made 10 awesome planets, instead of randomly generating endlessly the same things. Oh, and yes, there is not much to do in this game really and I’ve discovered over and over again the same technology (technology tree is very limited too).

If you're looking for a game that has vast economies, massive player fighting, and focuses on combat and a story but provides a shallow universe to do those things...

No Man's Sky isn't that game.

If you want difficult and extremely focused gameplay, a tightly focused story that's almost linear and short, and want combat over space exploration...

No Man's Sky isn't that game.

But then again, No Man's Sky never claimed to be that game.

Hello Games has been upfront about what NMS was from the beginning. A game about exploring the vastness of space while marveling at the wonder of it all. If you went into this game expecting a different game, and are raging about that... Then you should probably update your reading comprehension. It's in the fine print that it's not the game you want.

You know what? Not every game is gonna be what you want. You don't go into a Call of Duty game and cry that it doesn't have enough Barbie Princesses.
NMS is an amazing work for exactly what it is, and it deserves all the praise it gets.

If you know exactly what this game is, you can ignore the haters and jump in for probably hundreds of hours.

Whatever kerfluffle you might have heard about the launch of NMS, clear your mind of the noise. The game has changed on so many levels that it's obvious that the company loves the game, and continues to work towards the extremely lofty goals the team had set out for itself. Maybe you're still angry about how the game launched, and if you want to keep your anger and resentment, that's perfectly fine. But I think you're denying yourself a chance to play a game that is both fascinating and relaxing.

Now if you just don't like first person games, or games that aren't super action heavy all the time, then the game is likely not the game for you. Though to be honest, I almost always dislike first person perspective games, (I get motion sick usually), but for whatever reason, NMS doesn't trigger the motion sickness, and I like having a game I can play in a very relaxed pace.

One of the few games worthy of the Labor of Love award.

Hello Games made the game great over the past 7 years and they still haven't stopped.

Vote for it!

If you are looking for a fun space explorer, then this game isn't for you. It is very fun, exploration-y, and new for the first 6 hours. But after that, it gets very repetitive. Basically, the whole game is, "Okay, I need to harvest this mineral to create this device to create this device to create this device to create this device to create an upgrade for my ship that barely affects it, nevermind that it took me about 3-4 hours to get all of the needed materials to make it." Also, how do you refund games again?

[9/10] Besides a perfect track record of updates that over-delivered after the initial disappointing release, I just can't give NMS a perfect score because of two big reasons:

1. The building system is clunky, which makes building intricate structures rather difficult. It's been years since they've last updated the base building mechanics, I think they should improve the system somewhat. While on this topic, they should allow more stuff in the freighter base building. Perhaps less high-tech, cleaner-looking rooms?

2. They're still doing FOMO with expeditions.

There's nothing else to be said that hasn't been said before by others. It's a beautiful, serene game where you can waste an entire day exploring different planets, the storyline is great, the continuous updates are most welcome and laudable, the game has had very few bugs in my experience. I'd say they more than proved themselves, and while I'm not a fan of their upcoming game (I'm not a big fan of fantasy themes or dragons), I'd still be hyped for their future games. Still, don't pre-order anything. Ever.

No Man’s Sky has had one of the most impressive evolutions in recent years. At launch, it disappointed a lot of people by promising more than it delivered. But over time, Hello Games showed a rare level of commitment — they listened to the community, released dozens of free updates, and completely transformed the experience.

That said, the game still has some bugs that need fixing, which can be frustrating at times. I hope the team keeps paying attention to player feedback, just as they’ve done so far. Even so, it’s undeniable how much the game has grown and become an engaging experience — especially for those who enjoy exploration and science fiction, like I do.

edit 2023: Still good.

I finally sprung for this while it was on sale and holy cow I've been having so much fun.

Within a sci fi sandbox game, I love the prospect of exploring and then getting rewards for it, and that's a huge part of this game. For the most part it's mainly just cataloging the type of life something is or what its material composition is, which is a bit simple, but it works.

The core progression path for basically everything is based on modules. This means gradually outfitting your ship, multitool, exosuit, and later your exocraft and freighter with new equipment or boosts to existing pieces as you explore the universe and gather materials or make connections and learn how to communicate with other alien races.

Beyond exploring, scanning and shooting, there's a ton of subsystems in the game, and you can choose which ones you engage with. You're not forced to use a system you don't like. Some include settlement management, outpost construction, fishing, and fleet/frigate management and expeditions.

The weirdness you can discover is also fantastic. I've found planets where some animals look like tumbleweeds made of bone or are literal floating balls of energy, the entire environment appears in black and white, where giant worms plow through the ground, etc.

I almost wish I had picked this game up sooner; I haven't even gotten to the new corvette customization system yet and I've been having a blast.

No Mans Sky is a masterpiece that was once a flop. Not many game can come back from a massive failure, but No Mans Sky did and holy cow is it great. No Mans Sky is a massive (basically infinite) universe that you can explore. You might see a planet barely visible in the distance and you don’t have to teleport there; you can literally fly to it. It might take minutes, hours, days, possibly weeks (in real time) but luckily there is a hyper space like feature. You can mine, build bases, learn languages, build massive capital ships, discover new type of planets. Plants, creatures, and so much more. The possibilities are endless. The game is so vast that people are still discovering new things years later. Since No Mans Sky didn’t release this year; I can’t really vote for it on much, but I can vote for it for the Labor and Love award. No Mans Sky literally resurrected itself from the dead and still receives an absurd amount of content many years later. At the. Time of writing this review the game is $23.99. You should buy it. You won’t regret it……also vote for No Mans Sky for the Labor and Love award. (or is it the Labor of Love award. I can’t remember)

If you are looking for a 'cozy' game, but want a bit more structure that you can weave in and out of, this is it! I adore the blend of adventuring through the main story line, missions picked up at space stations or spending time harvesting/building on your own base. Having a game that can meet you where you are at day to day is a wonderful thing to have, and this game does that. 10/10.

The game is enjoyable on many fronts. The visuals are stunning, the ability to freely explore an infinite universe can be intimidating but also liberating, discovering alien ruins, unique ships, building a fleet of frigates. It's all great until you decide you want it all and realize you can't have it. Not unless you want to blow your brains out half way through. Kudos to the devs that keep coming up with new and interesting content to keep what is essentially an exploration game fresh.
BUT the amount of glitches and bugs, broken main quest lines and mini quests, and base building/farming objects that just don't work correctly is embarrassingly large. Normally I would have given a positive review but after 200+ hours of game play, waiting for glitches to be fixed and game objects to function correctly, it seems that they most likely never will.
It's an impressive game really but it still feels like it should still be in Beta because they keep releasing small and large content updates without fixing day one bugs.
